article.overview: A micrometeoroid protection experiment is an investigation of how to shield spacecraft, habitats, equipment and astronauts from the very small, very fast particles of interplanetary dust and debris that strike the Moon. The lunar surface has no atmosphere to slow these particles, so impacts can occur at hypervelocity speeds. This article covers the protection concepts and test programmes that the searches for this payload found in the published literature. The searches did not identify a flown lunar surface experiment dedicated to micrometeoroid protection. The designs discussed here are modelling baselines, engineering concepts, laboratory tests or funded research proposals [1][2][4][5].
article.description: Micrometeoroids are small particles of interplanetary material. The modelling study in [1] uses a mass range of 10^-6 g to 10 g when it calculates impact rates for a hypothetical ISS-sized lunar base at the south pole, using NASA's Meteoroid Engineering Model 3. A micrometeoroid protection experiment would test, demonstrate or model a way of reducing the damage such impacts cause. The protective system might be a metallic bumper with a rear wall, a layered shield, a thick layer of regolith, or a regolith-based composite. Three kinds of concept appear in the sources found for this article: a Whipple-type shield that the modelling study assumes as its baseline [1][6]; a regolith arch proposed by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory [4]; and regolith or regolith-composite materials tested in the laboratory or proposed for funded study [2][3][5]. Only the first of these is described in the literature as a shielding design for spacecraft, and this article does not verify its flight heritage.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of micrometeoroid protection work is to reduce the risk that impacts breach pressure walls, damage equipment or create hazardous ejecta. The modelling study in [1] estimates about 15,000 to 23,000 unshielded impacts per year on the hypothetical base, depending on location, and about 0.024 to 0.037 penetrating impacts per year when a Whipple-type shield is assumed. The Yates campaign [2][3] addresses ejecta rather than the primary impact: the thesis abstract states that meteoroid ejecta can travel farther than earlier assumptions suggested and names iron lithic fragments and impact feldspar spheres as the two most hazardous ejecta types [2]. The sources name lunar landers, habitats and spacesuits as the intended applications [2][3][4].
article.operating_principle: Hypervelocity protection works by converting the kinetic energy of a particle into fragmentation and spread-out energy absorption. In a Whipple-type design, the outer sacrificial plate breaks the projectile into a debris cloud and the rear wall must withstand the reduced threat, as is commonly described for this design. In a regolith design, the mass of the material itself slows and absorbs the particle. The JPL arch concept adds an outer high-strength blanket that fragments the projectile before the remains strike the regolith and its jacket [4]. In the Yates laboratory tests, regolith simulant and simulant-epoxy mixtures stopped simulated ejecta projectiles moving at or near lunar escape velocity, with penetration inside 3 cm [2]. The shields described in the sources are passive. None of the sources describes active control or power needs for the shield itself.
article.scientific_importance: Micrometeoroid protection is a design input for any long-duration lunar surface system, because impacts are a hazard to pressure walls, equipment and spacesuits. The modelling study [1] argues that a Whipple-type shield can cut the penetration threat by several orders of magnitude, but this is a model result that depends on the assumed shield and on the assumed meteoroid population. The Yates programme [2][3] is the most detailed experimental regolith impact study found in these searches. Its published abstract reports shallow penetration in simulant, but it does not give the full test data in the abstract. Taken together, the sources show that regolith shielding is being examined experimentally while layered metallic designs remain the main engineering baseline in the modelling literature [1][2].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a micrometeoroid protection experiment or shield. The examples below are different kinds of protection concept at different maturity levels. Values are given only where a source states them. The examples are not directly comparable: the Whipple-type entry is a modelling assumption, the JPL arch is a proposed concept, the Yates entry is a laboratory test with simulant, and the Stanford entry is a funded proposal with no reported results.

examples.name: Whipple-type bumper shield (modelling baseline)
examples.type: Engineering shielding concept used as the baseline in lunar-base impact modelling; flight heritage not verified here
examples.description: A Whipple-type shield places a thin outer sacrificial wall a short distance in front of a rear wall. The modelling study assumes this design as its baseline [1]. The paper states that state-of-the-art Whipple shields stop about 99.9997 per cent of micrometeoroids, which it describes as a reduction of nearly five orders of magnitude in threat [1]. This is a modelled result for the stated mass range and assumptions, not a measured performance. The NASA Johnson Space Center presentation on micrometeoroid environments and hypervelocity shields [6] was located but its abstract is unavailable, so no performance figures are taken from it.

facts.shielding_claim: About 99.9997 per cent of micrometeoroids stopped (modelled, state of the art, stated by the authors)
facts.status: Modelling assumption; flight heritage not verified in this run

examples.name: JPL ARMOR regolith arch concept
examples.type: Proposed concept (NASA Tech Brief, December 2012); no test or technology readiness statement found
examples.description: The concept is an arch-shaped shell of local regolith about 3 m thick, held in shape by a strong but deployable jacket, around a central cavity [4]. An external high-strength blanket is held over the jacket to absorb and fragment incoming projectiles, and the jacket and regolith absorb the remaining energy [4]. The Tech Brief claims that about 3 m of regolith would be sufficient against cosmic rays and solar protons, but gives no dose figures [4]. The Tech Brief calls the system near-term, but gives no test, prototype or readiness data [4].

facts.outer_blanket: High-strength blanket; material, thickness and standoff not given
facts.jacket: Strong but deployable material; not named
facts.status: Proposed concept; no test or readiness statement

examples.name: Yates regolith impact test campaign (LHS-1 simulant)
examples.type: Laboratory ground test with lunar highland simulant; not flight hardware
examples.description: Jacob Yates and collaborators fired projectiles from a two-stage light gas gun at lunar highland simulant LHS-1 and at a simulant-epoxy mixture at Texas A&M University's Hypervelocity Impact Laboratory [2][3]. The regolith was built up in 10 cm layers in a cylindrical target of about 5000 cm3 inside a vacuum chamber [3]. The thesis abstract reports that the regolith and simulant-epoxy mixtures stopped simulated ejecta at or near lunar escape velocity, with penetration inside 3 cm, and that aluminosilicate glass, aerogel and space shuttle tiles did not perform as well. It suggests layered designs such as Whipple shields as a next step [2]. The projectile speeds, sizes, simulant ratios and number of tests are not given in the abstract, and the trade article gives only qualitative findings [3].

examples.name: Regolith Biocomposite micrometeoroid shielding study (Stanford, NSTRF 2017)
examples.type: Funded research proposal; planned hypervelocity impact testing and modelling; no results reported
examples.description: The NASA project page describes Regolith Biocomposite (RBC), a biopolymer-stabilised regolith, as a candidate material for habitat shielding [5]. The stated objective is to raise its technology readiness from level 3 to level 5 through hypervelocity impact tests and hydrocode modelling [5]. The page reports no completed test data, model outputs or findings [5].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The only geometric value verified for these examples is the 3 m thickness of the JPL regolith shell [4]. The Tech Brief gives no cavity dimension, arch span or height. For the Yates campaign, a trade article reports a regolith bed of 5000 cm3 built in 10 cm layers, but it gives no bed diameter or depth [3]. No dimension is given in the sources for a Whipple-type shield in this context.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No mass value is verified for any example. The JPL concept is described only qualitatively as lowering launch mass compared with conventional structures [4]. No regolith mass, launch mass or shield areal mass is given in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is not publicly specified for any example in the sources reviewed. The JPL Tech Brief summary also includes an overview claim that the arch does not require continuous power or air pressure; that statement could not be checked against the full technical package and is not treated as established here [4].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The lunar surface has no substantial atmosphere, large surface temperature swings and exposure to radiation and micrometeoroid impacts. The JPL concept claims that about 3 m of regolith would protect against direct and secondary cosmic-ray and solar-proton radiation, and that the arch would reduce temperature swings by blocking direct sunlight [4]. No dose or temperature figures are given. The Yates tests were run in a vacuum chamber, which reproduces the lack of an atmosphere but not the lunar thermal environment [3]. A protective system also needs a stable mass of material that stays in place, and an outer layer that survives the environment. The sources do not give a site-specific micrometeoroid environment for any landing region; the modelling in [1] applies to one hypothetical south-pole base.
article.limitations: The main limitations are evidence gaps. The modelling in [1] is a preprint that assumes a Whipple-type shield, so the shield performance is a model input rather than a measurement, and regolith-based alternatives are not modelled. The Yates thesis abstract reports penetration inside 3 cm and qualitative failures, but the projectile speeds, sizes and number of tests are not stated in the abstract [2]. The trade-press description of the same campaign is secondary [3]. The JPL concept is documented only in a Tech Brief summary; the full technical package is behind a login, and its design details, test status and technology readiness are not verified [4]. The Stanford study reports planned tests and no results [5].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: No micrometeoroid protection experiment on the lunar surface has a verified delivery configuration in the sources found. The transport implications depend on the concept. A Whipple-type shield would be a structural add-on to a habitat or lander. The JPL arch would be built from local regolith rather than delivered as bulk mass, which is the basis of its claimed launch-mass advantage [4]. The laboratory campaign has no flight transport requirement [2][3].
transportation_process: For the JPL arch concept: place a deployable arch jacket on the surface with a temporary inflatable support [4].
Fill the jacket with local regolith; the inflatable supports the regolith during filling [4].
Once the arch is self-supporting, deflate and remove the inflatable [4].
Move habitat modules and equipment into the protected cavity [4].

For a Whipple-type shield on a habitat or lander: integrate the shield with the structure on Earth, launch and land it with the structure, and deploy nothing separately; no deployment sequence is described in the sources.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The JPL concept is described as autonomously assembled on site before the first crewed surface arrival [4]. The Tech Brief overview also mentions robotic deployment, which could not be verified in the full text. No deployment method is verified for a Whipple-type shield or for the Stanford regolith biocomposite.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No flown lunar micrometeoroid protection experiment was identified. The historical examples are laboratory impact tests with lunar simulants [2][3] and a funded study proposal [5]. Whipple-type shields are established in the orbital engineering literature and are the baseline assumed in [1]; their flight heritage was not verified in this research.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Not assessed. No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted, because no verified interface data for a named vehicle were found for any of these concepts.

article.historical_significance: The historical significance found so far is conceptual. The modelling in [1] and the proposals in [4][5] point to regolith and layered shields as options for lunar habitats. The Yates programme [2][3] is the most recent experimental regolith impact study identified here. Earlier mission-specific micrometeoroid protection hardware was not verified in this run.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name describes a class of research rather than one instrument. Two different projects share the abbreviation ARMOR and must not be confused: the JPL 'Archway for Radiation and Micrometeorite Occurrence Resistance' concept [4], and the Yates 'Advanced Research in Moon Operations and Resiliency' test campaign [2][3]. The impact rates in [1] are model results for an assumed population, location and shield. The Yates results are taken from the thesis abstract and a trade article, not from the full test data. Whipple shield performance and ISS-related shielding claims seen in search snippets were not checked against full primary text, so they are not used as facts in this article.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image URLs were verified, so none are listed.

data_quality_notes: No flown lunar surface micrometeoroid protection experiment was identified in the searches; the article covers concepts, models, laboratory tests and proposals.
The Whipple-type shield performance (about 99.9997 per cent stopped) is a modelled result from a preprint that assumes the shield; it is not a measurement.
ARMOR is used for two different projects: the JPL Archway concept (NPO-47686) and the Yates Advanced Research in Moon Operations and Resiliency campaign. They are kept separate.
The Yates campaign figures come from the thesis abstract and a trade article; projectile speeds, sizes, simulant ratios and test counts were not verified from the full text.
The NTRS PDFs for the 2012 ARMOR technical report and the 2019 hypervelocity impact overview could not be read as text; no figures are taken from them.
Stuffed Whipple shield and ISS module performance claims seen only in search snippets were not verified and are not used as facts.
The Electrodynamic Dust Shield (dust protection, not micrometeoroid protection) was seen only in search snippets and is not described in this article.
No images were verified from official pages; no image URLs are included.
Transportation compatibility with any named lander, rover or spacecraft was not verified and is not asserted.
